# LaunchSense

LaunchSense checks the codebase, not the business. The website is the public read: paste a GitHub URL, get a plain report. A coding tool calls the same public read at the hosted MCP address. You do not clone this repo to use it.

This stage is alpha. Alpha has no login for the public read: the hosted MCP address works with no credential. An auth slot exists and is not enforced. A LaunchSense credential is optional and is how the hosted read is attributed.

## Connect

```
https://harmless-chihuahua-667.convex.site/mcp
```

Cursor adds that URL under `mcpServers.launchsense`. Claude Code:

```
claude mcp add launchsense --transport http https://harmless-chihuahua-667.convex.site/mcp
```

The client POSTs one JSON-RPC message. The server returns one JSON answer, or a `text/event-stream` when the client asks for one.

## Tools

`launchsense_scan_public` takes `repoUrl` like `https://github.com/owner/repo`. It reads that public repo on our server. Guest limits of 200 files and about 2MB apply. OSV covers up to 50 packages. deps.dev is not asked. The hosted read keeps 200 scans an hour for the shared hosted bucket, and 600 in total across the hosted lane, then the route pauses. The counter holds no part of your network address. Sending a LaunchSense credential in an `Authorization` header is optional. When one resolves, the per-tool caps are 20 scans an hour and 120 in a day, counted against that credential's own bucket. Those per-tool numbers are a policy choice with no traffic measurement behind them. A credential that is presented and refused gets no scan, rather than being treated as anonymous.

`launchsense_get_report` takes `scanId` and returns the coverage line and the findings.

Those two names belong to this address. The local server under Surfaces has its own names, and its `launchsense_scan_public_notice` scans nothing: it only points back here.

A partial result is not a pass. This address does not read a repo that exists only on a laptop. A private repo uses Sign in on the website.

## Checks

Fixed checks cover secrets, code shapes, dependency names, license text, dependency license terms, and project hygiene, plus duplicate files and large files.

### The licence declaration

For a project that commits an npm `package-lock.json` with a `packages` map, every installed package, direct and transitive, is read for the licence it declares. The lockfile is the declaration being read, so this costs no extra request and adds no new egress. Where the lockfile has no `license` field and an installed `package.json` is available to the caller, that manifest is the fallback, and a lockfile that disagrees with it reads as Unknown. A declaration that is not an SPDX expression, such as `MIT/X11`, reads as Unknown. `UNLICENSED` reads as `LicenseRef-Proprietary-UNLICENSED`, which is a proprietary claim and not the Unlicense dedication. An `OR` expression stays a choice and attaches no obligation from either id. A bare `GPL-2.0` is kept as declared and marked deprecated, because rewriting it into `-only` would assert an only-versus-or-later choice the string does not make. `GPL-2.0+` normalizes to `GPL-2.0-or-later`.

`license.inventory` is an informational row carrying the per-id counts, the count of unknowns, and the named gaps. `license.declaration` is one informational row whose fingerprint is the licence mix itself, so a change between two permissive licences still moves a fingerprint and shows up on the rescan. `license.dependency` is one row per component whose terms a person must read, low for file-level copyleft and medium for library copyleft, strong copyleft, source-available, and proprietary terms. The per-component rows are capped at 25 per scan and the number left out is stated. An Unknown licence never produces a row and never carries a severity.

`shared/licensing/obligations.ts` holds one cited row per licence family: licence text, copyright notice, a NOTICE file where the licence has one, state of changes, source disclosure for copyleft, and the distribution clash for strong copyleft. It is a table of what a licence text asks for. It is not a legal engine, it does not model linking or aggregation, and it does not decide whether an obligation applies to how you ship.

`npm run notices` writes the third-party notice artifact from the committed lockfile. Same lockfile in, byte-identical file out. The local review carries the same text. It is a declaration of what each dependency says its licence is, and it names what it did not read.

On a rescan, a dependency whose declared licence changed is reported through the existing transition machinery as `license_change`, so a re-licensed package shows up on the comparison rather than only when the tree was first read. A dependency that was added or removed is still a code change.

The guarded AI lookup runs only for an Unknown licence, only when a lane is supplied, and only with the package name, the version, and fixed wording in the prompt. The result is a suggestion. It has no rule id, no fingerprint, and no severity, and it never writes into the component it came from. No lane is wired in this release, so the path is refused and unknown stays unknown.

Not checked on any surface: yarn.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml, Cargo, Go and PyPI dependency licences, a vendored tree, a per-file SPDX header or REUSE.toml, and registry freshness. A lockfile with no `packages` map reads as incomplete, not as zero licences.

License lines are signals, not legal advice. Unknown stays unknown. A model may quote one next look. That quote is not a finding. The priority table always orders the report. The decision API may reorder inside one severity band. The model does not choose which findings exist. Plain-word rewriting and that reorder are in the product and still evolving. No writing provider is configured in this release, so fixed wording is what ships. A reinforcement learning loop, based on what a later scan shows as fixed or still broken, is the next step. It is not a trained model, and it does not train on the code.

## Surfaces

Three notes on surfaces. The first two are not the hosted address:

- A local stdio MCP server (`mcp/main.go`, wired by `install.sh`) reviews a checkout on that machine. The Go module is `mcp/`, and there is no `go.mod` at the repo root, so it starts with `cd mcp && go run .`. `install.sh` writes that command for Cursor, with `cwd` set to the `mcp` folder. It needs Go on `PATH`; without Go the installer says so and registers no server. It is for a checkout of this repository, not for the public address.
  - It speaks MCP over stdio as newline-delimited JSON: one JSON message per line in, one JSON message per line out, with no length header. `initialize` answers with protocol version 2024-11-05. Refused and error lines go to stderr, so stdout carries protocol only.
  - One message may be up to 4 MiB (4,194,304 bytes, the trailing newline included). A longer line is answered with a JSON-RPC error, nothing runs, and the next message is still answered.
  - Its tools are `launchsense_scan_repo`, which reviews the checkout and takes no arguments, `launchsense_report`, which asks the hosted API for a report by scan id, `launchsense_github`, which reports the local `gh` login, and `launchsense_scan_public_notice`, which scans nothing and only names where the public read lives. A tool name this server does not have is a protocol error, so the hosted name `launchsense_scan_public` called here is refused rather than answered with a scan. A missing, wrong-typed, or undeclared argument is refused rather than ignored.
  - `launchsense_scan_repo` reviews `LAUNCHSENSE_ROOT`, which `install.sh` sets to the checkout root, so it reads the checkout and not the `mcp` folder. With `LAUNCHSENSE_ROOT` unset it reads the checkout above a `mcp` module folder, and otherwise the folder it was started in. `LAUNCHSENSE_ROOT` must be absolute, and a folder that is not a checkout is named in the answer.
  - A report body over 1 MiB comes back marked partial and is never returned as a whole report. An API call gives up after 8 seconds and the local review after 10 minutes, so a call that hangs ends in an error instead of holding the session open.
  - It reads files locally and does not upload them. Usage counts are off unless you answer yes to one question. `install.sh` asks before it records anything and defaults to no; it keeps the answer, with the wording it agreed to, in `~/.config/launchsense/consent.jsonl`. With a yes it sends rule id counts, the harness name, the version, how long it took, and which order source ran. That share carries no code, paths, titles, or function names. `install.sh --enterprise` and `LAUNCHSENSE_DIAGNOSTICS=off` leave it off. The notice for all of this is at `/privacy` and in `docs/PRIVACY.md`.
- A GitHub App installation-token minter (`convex/github/app.ts`) mints a short-lived installation token. No scan flow calls it yet; the connected GitHub App read is roadmap, not built.
- The hosted usage route (`POST /api/mcp/usage`) writes counts only. It needs a deployment secret header, `x-launchsense-usage-key`. When `USAGE_ROUTE_KEY` is unset, it rejects every caller.

Two tables, `usageMeters` and `connectedInstallations`, are defined in the schema but have no reader yet. No query returns them.

## Credentials

The hosted routes accept an optional LaunchSense credential in `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. A token is `ls_live_<publicId>_<secret>`. The server keeps the `publicId` in the clear as the lookup prefix and a SHA-256 hash of the whole token, never the token. Resolution is one indexed read on the `publicId`, then a constant-time compare of the hash. `revoked` and `revokedAt` are read on every resolve, so a revoke is immediate.

Three layers, kept apart in the code and in the schema:

- `callerId` is the `credentials` row id, server-minted from the token. It is the only layer with authority: quota, attribution, and scan ownership read it.
- `declaredHarness` is a label an operator records at issuance. It is a claim. It never enters a rate limit key, an ownership check, or an access decision.
- `verifiedBinding` is a server-observed fact tying a credential to a person or an installation. It is absent on every row today and that is honest, not a gap being papered over: a scan reads the public repository with our own GitHub credential, so nothing about the call identifies a person. A GitHub App installation path would produce one. Until then every harness-level number is a caller claim.

The token carries an audience, the canonical MCP server URI `https://harmless-chihuahua-667.convex.site/mcp`, and the server checks it, so a credential minted elsewhere is refused. A 401 carries `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata=".../.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp"`. That metadata document is not served yet, and the header names no issuer, because there is no authorization server behind this. Nothing authenticates on `Mcp-Session-Id`, and no session id is issued. `Authorization` is in `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` so a browser client can send one.

Issuance is a server or admin step with no UI: `internal.identity.store.mintCredential` is an internal mutation, there is no public function that mints a credential, and no route accepts one. The token is returned exactly once and cannot be recovered afterwards.

The migration path changes only where the token comes from: OAuth 2.1 with this server as the resource server, RFC 9728 discovery, RFC 8707 audience binding, and the token's `sub` becomes `callerId`. Every downstream part is already in the shape that migration needs.

## Attribution

`scans` records `attributedCallerId`, `channel` (`web`, `mcp`, `api`), `surface` (`web`, `mcp_hosted`), `commitSha`, and `treeSha`. `attributed` is written `false` on a scan with no or refused credential rather than left off, so attributed over total is a real ratio and dropping an unscanned row cannot inflate it. `runScan` is the browser door and takes `repoUrl` and nothing else; `runHostedScan` is the internal door the hosted routes call and adds only identity. Both call one implementation, so there is one enforcement point, not two.

`commitSha` and `treeSha` are separate because they are different values: `GET /git/trees/{sha}` returns the tree object sha, not the commit sha. The commit response already carries `commit.tree.sha`, so the tree response is compared against it at no extra request, and a disagreement fails the scan instead of recording a snapshot neither response supports. The tree URL and every blob ref are built through functions that refuse anything that is not a full 40-character commit sha, so a branch name cannot reach a read.

`findInFlight` used to match on (owner, repo) with no sha and no identity, and `runScan` handed that row back once a sha was pinned, so two callers scanning the same public repository shared one row and the second received a scan belonging to the first. It now only reuses a row that belongs to the caller. Anything else is skipped, the caller mints its own row, and the 24h sha-keyed tree cache copies the tree into it, so the work is not repeated.

The headline metric is distinct `callerId` values with at least one scan in the trailing 7 days, counted only over scans where a credential resolved. The rescan rate is attributed callers with 2 or more distinct shas for the same repo within 28 days, over attributed callers with at least one scan in that window. The fields both metrics need are recorded on `scans`; no rollup emits these two metric rows yet, so neither number exists as data today. The hourly cap is 20 and the per-day cap is 120, a starting policy with no traffic measurement behind them; whether they are the right numbers is unknown until measured.

## Analytics

Two tables, and one nightly fold.

- `usageEvents` holds one row per MCP protocol action on the hosted address: `initialize`, `tools/list`, `tools/call`. It is the only table this lane writes per call.
- `dailyMetrics` is the rollup. One row per (day, metric, low-cardinality dims). There is no dashboard yet; when one exists it reads this table and nothing else.
- `rollupDaily` runs at 03:20 UTC and folds yesterday. It replaces the day rather than appending, so a retried cron cannot double count.
- `purgeExpiredUsageEvents` runs at 03:40 UTC and deletes `usageEvents` rows past 30 days, bounded at 500 rows a run and reporting when it hits that bound. Separate from the fold because a Convex mutation cannot call another mutation.
- `scans.surface` is written on both paths: `web` for the browser flow, `mcp_hosted` for the hosted MCP route and the JSON API. `scans.channel` separates the two hosted doors, `mcp` for `/mcp` and `api` for `/api/mcp/scan`.

The north star is `repos_with_proven_fix`: distinct repositories where a `findingTransitions` row says `state=fixed` and `cause=code_change` and both endpoint scans reached `status=completed`. A fix counted as `advisory_update` or `analyzer_update` is this product shipping a rule pack, so those are three separate metrics from day one and never folded in.

Two guardrails. `partial_coverage_rate` is partial over all analyzed, split by `truncated`, `tree_truncated`, and `errorKind`. `regression_after_fix_rate` is the share of proven fixes whose `ruleId` came back in the next completed scan of the same repo. Both are lower bounds where the read window runs out, and the code says so.

What is never collected, enforced in code by `convex/analytics/privacy.ts`: file content, paths, findings titles, snippets, raw error text, secrets, IP addresses, model names, prompt text, and the OTel Opt-In attributes `gen_ai.tool.call.arguments`, `gen_ai.tool.call.result`, `gen_ai.prompt.variable.*`, and `mcp.resource.uri`. The argument to a scan tool is a repository URL, which is the reason the Opt-In is refused rather than merely not required. `repoKey` is `HMAC(deployment salt, day + "owner/repo")` or absent; the salt comes from `ANALYTICS_DAY_SALT`, so same-day joins work and nothing joins across days. `clientName` goes through a fixed eight-value allowlist, because `clientInfo.name` is client-declared and storing it raw would let one caller mint a new dimension per request.

Names it will not segment on: a repository. The rollup counts distinct repos while it runs and stores only the count, so a stored day cannot be joined back to a repo. Per-rule and per-severity fix breakdowns are not on `dailyMetrics`: `findingTransitions` holds them, and a per-rule dimension would multiply rows for a few hundred numbers.

## Do not claim

The review does not say the app will sell. It does not edit the repo. It does not certify anything. It does not treat a source-available license as open source.
